paragraphs.heading: Picking up my mom at the airport
paragraphs.edited: Imagine I ask you to pick up my mom tomorrow at the airport. Do you think you could find her? No chance. What if I said my mom is coming into the airport tomorrow, into Los Angeles International Airport? Could you find her? Still probably not. But what if I said she arrives at 3:42 p.m. on flight 1717 from Dallas? Oh, and by the way, here's a picture of my mom. Could you find her? Of course. What's the difference? In this last instance I gave you specific details to recognize my mom when she arrived.

paragraphs.heading: Details about the coming Messiah
paragraphs.edited: This is not too different from what God does in the Old Testament in preparation for the coming Messiah, who would be the Savior and liberator of the Jewish people and ultimately of everyone. When Jesus physically walked on earth, it had been hundreds of years since the last Old Testament book was written. After his resurrection, Jesus was talking to his disciples. Luke 24 reports that he talks to them and says, don't you understand that Moses and the prophets of the Old Testament were speaking of me? Jesus consistently understood his life as fulfilling the people and events and prophecies of the Old Testament. There are roughly 300 prophecies from the Old Testament, ranging from the minor to the major, that Jesus fulfilled. Let's briefly consider five of them.

paragraphs.heading: Born in Bethlehem
paragraphs.edited: First, the minor prophet Micah said the Messiah would be born in the small town of Bethlehem and would have divine status. "As for you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, seemingly insignificant among the clans of Judah, from you a king will emerge who will rule over Israel on my behalf, one whose origins are in the distant past." And as Matthew 2:1 reports, Jesus was born in Bethlehem, a small town of only a few hundred.

paragraphs.heading: From David's line, and working miracles
paragraphs.edited: 2 Samuel 7 says that the Messiah would be from the line of David, the king. In Romans 1:3, Paul confirms that Jesus was in fact a descendant of David. Isaiah 35:5-6 says that the Messiah would perform miracles, give sight to the blind, heal the sick, and more. And each of the Gospels reports that Jesus went from town to town performing these remarkable miracles.

paragraphs.heading: Galilee, and a messenger before him
paragraphs.edited: Isaiah 9:1 indicates that his ministry would be in the region of Galilee, and again, as the Gospels consistently report, Jesus spent a considerable amount of his time ministering in the region of Galilee. Malachi 3:1 says a messenger would precede him, and as Mark 1:3 reveals, John the Baptist prepared the way for Jesus.

paragraphs.heading: Did the writers invent this?
paragraphs.edited: You might be thinking, the Gospel writers intentionally crafted their message to fit Messianic expectations. But this doesn't work, for at least two reasons. First, why would the apostles invent a view of Jesus as Messiah they knew was false, and then be willing to suffer and die for it? The fact that they were willing to suffer and die for Jesus as Messiah shows that they were not making him up. They had nothing to gain. Second, while Jesus did fulfill Old Testament Messianic expectations, the way he fulfilled them surprised some people. Why would the apostles have invented a dying and rising Messiah, a Messiah who was crucified as a criminal, if they were trying to reach the Jews? Such an invention would have been counterproductive to their message.

paragraphs.heading: Taken out of context?
paragraphs.edited: Some skeptics also push back and say, wait a minute, the prophecies are taken out of context. For example, the Gospel of Matthew cites Hosea 11:1, in which it says, "out of Egypt I will call my son." Well, in its original context that was the nation of Israel being brought out of slavery in Egypt, but Matthew applies it to Jesus. Is this a mistaken, out-of-context, false prophecy? Well, we need to keep in mind how the Jews would often interpret different passages. Sometimes there was a one-to-one correspondence, such as the Messiah being born in Bethlehem. Other times there was a type or foreshadowing from the Old Testament that was deeper fulfilled in the Messiah. And in this case, Israel was brought out of Egypt in the same way that Jesus brings people out of slavery, then and even now.

paragraphs.heading: Like never having seen winter
paragraphs.edited: It's easy to see how some Jewish scholars have had a different expectation of the coming Messiah, since they interpreted many of the prophecies differently. They didn't have the hindsight, the value of looking back, that we have today. Think of it this way. What if you were given all these signs that the seasons were changing: leaves changing color, then falling to the ground, the air getting cooler, the nights getting longer. Imagine seeing this happen, yet you had never seen or experienced winter before. You'd be pretty surprised to wake up and see snow on the ground. In hindsight it would start to make sense. In fact, you would begin to see the signs come into focus.

paragraphs.edited: We are fortunate today to be able to look back on the Old Testament and see the hundreds of prophecies fulfilled in the life and death and ministry of Jesus. When we look at the Old Testament through the lens of the person of Jesus, we can see that he in fact is the long-awaited Messiah.
